newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks buffeted in another volitile session.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks buffeted in another volitile session.

text.p: Japanese stocks were buffeted in another volatile session on Tuesday, falling sharply and then rebounding in what traders say may represent the end of the frenzied selling -- at least for now.
Brokers say last-minute investor buying of blue chips rescued the benchmark share average from its initial loss of over 500 points scored in early trading.

"Domestic investors, including pension funds and some foreign investors, started buying bellwether issues near the end of the session, helping erase the losses accumulated in the morning," said Dai-ichi Securities analyst Akishige Ishikura.
The benchmark Nikkei average of 225 leading shares closed just 25.66 points or 0.14 percent lower at 18,093.13. Its March futures closed down 120 points at 18,010.

Stocks rocketed to close over 800 points higher on Monday in reaction to the drastic falls in the previous week and media reports that a senior official of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party called for steps to rescue weak stock prices.

But the bubble of enthusiasm was popped on Tuesday morning by remarks from Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto made late on Monday that economic fundamentals were not bad and by the fact that he made no mention of special measures to prop up stocks.
Despite the rebound, many brokers said that perils of a resumed tumble remain, and that only the government could set the market back on its feet.
"What the government needs to do is to take swift action to realise structural reforms in the economy," Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute said.
Takagi said the government must take some action such as abolishing the securities transaction tax as early as April, and seek early implementation of Japan's planned "Big Bang" financial reforms.

Some traders said the market may having already hit its near-term floor, but said it is still vulnerable to renewed selling pressure due to lingering worries over the health of the economy and the debt-burdened banking sector.

Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities, said that judging from the rebound on Monday and the healthy turnover on the first two days of the week, the Nikkei average may have settle down, at least for now.
"There is likely to be more weakness in February before book-closing and especially if high-flying U.S. stocks start to falter," he said.
Technical analysts say that the market appears to have found a support line just above the 17,000 point level.

"A sharp rebound after a nose-dive forms a bottom on charts," said Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd. "Although the market environment is still unclear, the Nikkei could remain on a recovery trend for now."
Analysts see key support at around 17,303 points, the Nikkei's closing low on Friday, or around 17,019, the intra-day low on Monday, which are 17-month lows.

They said stocks could retest these levels sometime in February, as the market still lacks confidence in Japan's economic recovery, adding that a break through the floor could trigger an accelerated drop to new depths.
Banking and securities shares, haunted by bad debt problems, were hit by renewed rounds of selling, brokers said.

The dollar, meanwhile, was clawing its way back up again against the yen on Tuesday after falling earlier on remarks by Toyota Motor president that an appropriate dollar/yen level would be 100-110 yen. It hovered at about 116.50 yen in late Tokyo trading against its New York close of 116.50 on Monday.
Japanese government bond (JGB) futures ended a bit higher with the key March contract up 0.06 at 125.73.
